extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/anthropology interested in theories of sexual love and instinct (e.g., Schopenhauer scholarship)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Schopenhauer's criteria and explanatory principles about sexual love, attraction, and instinct as presented in a philosophical/textbook excerpt. Focuses on the factors that guide sexual choice and the physiological, psychological, and metaphysical rationale offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual pleasure as disguised instinct (interest of the species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual pleasure is merely a disguised instinct (i.e., sense of the species) which strives to maintain its type; individuals are deceived by an illusion making them think they pursue their own end while serving the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding examples: bird building nest, insect laying eggs or providing food for larvae, bees/wasps/ants building complex economies. The illusion conceals the service of the species under the mask of an egotistical end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological basis of instinct: ganglion (subjective) vs cerebral (objective) system
rubrics_metrics.description: In creatures governed by instinct there is a preponderance of the ganglion (subjective nervous) system over the cerebral (objective) system; they are moved more by subjective ideas exciting desire than by proper objective apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This physiological arrangement explains why instinctive behavior appears as an illusion of self-interested pleasure while serving species-level ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy appetite as a specific female instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Pregnant women's capricious appetites arise from special modifications of the blood required by the embryo; certain foods producing such modification present themselves as objects of ardent longing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as an example of an instinct unique to women (an 'extra' instinct) tied to physiological needs of reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender difference in development of instincts (women have more developed ganglion system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women possess a more developed ganglion system than men and therefore display certain instinctual tendencies (e.g., pregnancy cravings) more strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain sex differences in instinctive behavior and attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differing constancy: men inclined to inconstancy, women to constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: By nature man is inclined to inconstancy in love (longing for variety); woman is inclined to constancy (attachment increases after satisfaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by reproductive capacities: man can impregnate many, woman limited to roughly one child/year — thus nature moves woman to retain nourisher/protector; faithfulness is 'artificial' for men, 'natural' for women; adultery by women is both objectively more consequential and subjectively more unnatural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age as primary absolute consideration for sexual choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice generally accepts ages from menarche to menopause, with decided preference for ages 18–28 (for attraction); outside those years women who no longer menstruate excite aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconscious end is reproductive possibility; attraction declines in proportion to removal from fittest reproductive age; 'youth without beauty' still attracts; beauty without youth does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health as an absolute consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Acute diseases only temporarily disturb attraction; chronic diseases or cachexia repel because they are transmissible to offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health signals suitability for producing healthy offspring; chronic illness is an anti-pattern for sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton/figure (structural conformation) as essential consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The skeleton is the basis of the species' type; deformity or a crooked figure repels, while a straight figure is highly valued; even 'ugly' faces with straight figures preferred over beautiful faces with deformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disproportion of skeleton (e.g., stunted, dumpy, short-boned) and halting gait are strongly repulsive unless caused by accident. A strikingly beautiful figure can nevertheless compensate for other defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallness of the feet as species-characteristic beauty criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Small feet are valued because they are an essential characteristic of the human species (associated with upright gait); cited culturally (Sirach) as a mark of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/cultural justification used to explain emphasis on particular anatomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teeth as important hereditary and functional feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Teeth are important because they are essential for nourishment and are specifically hereditary, thus valued in sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional-hereditary linkage explains emphasis on dental features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulness of flesh indicating nutritive/plastic capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain fulness of flesh (predominance of vegetative/plastic function) signals abundant nourishment for the fetus; extreme leanness repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Body fat distribution interpreted as indicator of reproductive/nutritional fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full female bosom as special charm (nursing signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A full female bosom exerts exceptional charm on males because it promises abundant nourishment to the newborn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, excessive fat excites disgust (interpreted as uterine atrophy/barrenness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial bone structure and parts of the face (nose, mouth, chin, eyes, forehead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial beauty is evaluated chiefly by underlying bones: an aesthetically pleasing nose, small mouth (small maxillae), a prominent chin (mentum prominulum) and beautiful eyes/forehead are decisive; certain deviations (e.g., turned-up nose, receding chin) spoil attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eyes and forehead are linked to psychical/intellectual qualities inherited (esp. from the mother). Small maxillae and certain bone shapes are described as specifically human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women’s absolute/typical age preference and priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Women generally prefer men aged about 30–35 (over youths) and prioritize strength and courage more than facial beauty; they value qualities promising strong offspring and a protector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women attend less to beauty of face and more to physical strength/courage (qualities inherited from father); women can 'compensate' many defects via reproduction except for qualities peculiar to the male sex (broad shoulders, beard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychical qualities attracting women (character over intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are instinctively attracted to qualities of heart and character in men—firmness of will, decision, courage, honesty, good-heartedness—whereas intellectual gifts do not exert direct instinctive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary mental endowment might even be unfavorable; intellect can be used artificially (arts, languages) to increase attractiveness rather than being the root instinctive attractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (individual) considerations: complementarity and neutralisation of defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative considerations aim to correct or neutralize the chooser's own deviations from the species' type—'each one loves what he lacks'—leading to strong, exclusive passion when complements align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: two persons must neutralize each other like acid and alkali to form a neutral salt. The neutralisation requires matching definite degrees of manhood/womanhood so one's one-sidedness is exactly annulled by the other's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-matching of sexual characteristics (one-sidedness correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every individual’s degree of manhood or womanhood should correspond to the other's degree so that each one's one-sidedness exactly annuls the other's; the most manly man seeks the most womanly woman, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological spectrum (from gynander to androgyne to hermaphrodite) underlies compatibility; extreme mismatches produce sterility or unfitness to propagate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction-by-opposites in specific traits (size, complexion, parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to prefer mates who are the corrective opposite of their own defects—for example, little men preferring big women, snub-nosed individuals preferring hook-noses, blondes preferring brunettes—especially for important body parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference strength depends on importance of trait; sometimes 'ugly' people are loved when their abnormities exactly correct the other's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament complementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperaments act analogously: each tends to prefer the temperament opposed to his own, in proportion to how pronounced his own temperament is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person very 'perfect' in one respect will not seek imperfection there, but tolerates it more easily; complementarity fosters passionate attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative scrutiny as species-level meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: The intense, searching inspection lovers perform when first meeting is the 'meditation of the genius of the species'—an unconscious review of features to judge suitability for producing the species' next individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scrutiny explains capriciousness and keen attention to every excess or defect; discovery of an overlooked disqualifying trait can extinguish yearning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualisation intensifies love; mere sexual impulse is ignoble
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensity of love increases with individualisation: sexual impulse directed to all is base and quantitative; when directed to a single individual (individualised), the species' aim regarding quality is served and passion can reach vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly individualized love can make all other goods and even life lose value and may lead to extreme sacrifices, madness, or suicide if frustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphysical explanation: will to live objectifying in a definite individual
rubrics_metrics.description: An intense passion may be due to the 'will' desiring to objectify itself in a perfectly definite individual producible only by this pair; lovers imagine personal desire but in truth the will to live seeks to realize a metaphysical end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why love often arises at first sight and why its fulfilment extinguishes the passion—if the metaphysical end (e.g., fertility) is frustrated (e.g., woman barren), passion may also be extinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-interest can override social norms (jealousy, sacrifice, adultery)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the species' interest (sexual love) is at stake, honour, duty, and social scruples are readily set aside; passionate lovers act 'by nature' as if they belong to each other by divine right, sometimes committing adultery or sacrificing honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: literary and religious references (Calderon, Chamfort, Gospel anecdote) are used to illustrate indulgence or suspension of ordinary moral constraints in face of species-level drives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive capacity asymmetry underpins behavioral differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative reproductive asymmetry (man can beget many children; woman typically one child/year) explains differing evolutionary pressures: male promiscuity vs female selectivity/constancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demographic/physiological fact is used repeatedly to ground claims about fidelity, selection priorities, and moral evaluations.
